content: Serum sickness is an immune system reaction that mimics an allergic response. It occurs when the immune system reacts to certain medications, injected proteins used for treating immune conditions, or antiserum. Antiserum is the liquid component of blood containing antibodies that protect against infectious or toxic substances. Symptoms of Serum Sickness The symptoms of serum sickness include fever, a general feeling of being unwell, hives, itching, joint pain, rash, and swollen lymph nodes. These symptoms typically appear 7 to 21 days after the initial exposure to antiserum or medication. However, individuals previously exposed to the substance may develop symptoms within 1 to 3 days. Causes of Serum Sickness Plasma, the clear fluid portion of blood, contains proteins such as antibodies that are part of the immune response to infections. Antiserum is derived from the plasma of individuals or animals with immunity to specific infections or toxins. It is used to provide immediate, temporary protection (passive immunization) to individuals exposed to dangerous microorganisms, such as tetanus or rabies, while their body develops an active immune response. In serum sickness, the immune system mistakenly identifies a protein in the antiserum as a harmful antigen. This triggers an immune response, forming immune complexes that cause inflammation and other symptoms. Certain medications, such as penicillin, cefaclor, and sulfa drugs, can also cause similar reactions. Unlike typical drug allergies, which occur shortly after re-exposure, serum sickness develops 7 to 21 days after the first exposure to the medication. Injected proteins like antithymocyte globulin (used for organ transplant rejection) and rituximab (used for immune disorders and cancers) can also trigger serum sickness. Blood products may similarly cause this reaction. When to Seek Medical Care You should contact your healthcare provider if you develop symptoms of serum sickness within four weeks of receiving medication or antiserum. Diagnosis Enlarged and tender lymph nodes may be present. Urine tests may reveal blood or protein, and blood tests may show immune complexes or signs of blood vessel inflammation. Treatment Options Treatment for serum sickness includes corticosteroid creams or ointments and other soothing skin medications to relieve itching and rash. Antihistamines can reduce the duration of illness and alleviate rash and itching. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen or naproxen, may help relieve joint pain. In severe cases, oral corticosteroids like prednisone may be prescribed. The medication or antiserum causing the reaction should be discontinued, and future use of the offending substance should be avoided. Prognosis Symptoms of serum sickness usually resolve within a few days. Possible Complications If the medication or antiserum that caused serum sickness is used again in the future, the risk of experiencing a similar reaction is significantly increased. Potential complications include: Anaphylactic shock, a life-threatening, immediate allergic reaction. Inflammation of the blood vessels. Swelling of the face, arms, and legs. Prevention There is no known way to prevent the development of serum sickness. Individuals who have experienced serum sickness, anaphylactic shock, or drug allergies should avoid future use of the offending antiserum or drug.
